specAnchors.text: understand how the formulae of simple compounds can be obtained experimentally, including metal oxides, water and salts containing water of crystallisation
calculate empirical and molecular formulae from experimental data

primer.text: The last few notes turned masses into moles and moles back into masses using relative formula masses. This note points that arithmetic at the laboratory bench: measure masses before and after a reaction, convert both into moles, and the ratio that falls out is the formula itself. The worked case is a salt that carries water inside its crystals.

modules.title: Formulae of Simple Compounds by Experiment
sourceHeadings: Formulae of Simple Compounds by Experiment
Formulae of a simple compound by experiment
modules.opening: A chemical formula can be dug out of the laboratory itself: weigh the substances before and after a reaction, convert both masses into moles, and compare the two. Experiments where a gas escapes or is taken up suit this treatment best, because the mass change is easy to see. The ratio of moles then hands you the empirical formula.
keyPoints: Mass measurements taken before and after a reaction are the raw material for a formula.
Converting the masses into moles lets molar ratios be deduced, and the ratios give the empirical formula.
Experiments with gases being lost or gained are the easiest to handle this way.
Heating a hydrated salt drives its water off as vapour, shrinking the mass by exactly the water's contribution.
The formulae of metal oxides, water and salts holding water of crystallisation can all be found experimentally.

low.restatement: Before the reaction, weigh everything; afterwards, weigh again. The difference is the mass that left as gas, and the two remaining masses convert into moles for the ratio.
low.analogy: It works like counting a leaky delivery: weigh the van full and again at the end, and whatever vanished on the road is exactly what the journey consumed.
low.examPointer: When a question says 'a gas is lost', read it as an invitation to use the mass change rather than a warning that the data is broken.

medium.restatement: The bench method and the arithmetic method are the same move at different scales: balances supply the masses, relative formula masses turn them into moles, and the mole ratio is the formula, straight from evidence.
medium.analogy: Think of a baker deducing a recipe from the flour gone missing and the bread that appeared: the pantry's losses and gains, weighed carefully, expose the proportions.
medium.examPointer: Questions usually hand you the masses; the marks sit in dividing by the right relative formula masses and simplifying the ratio without panic.

modules.title: The Formula of a Hydrated Salt
sourceHeadings: The formula of a hydrated salt
modules.opening: Copper sulfate crystals are blue because they hold water; heat them and the blue gives way to a white powder as steam escapes. Weighing before and after captures the water's mass, and dividing each remaining mass by its relative formula mass exposes the ratio of salt to water - the x in the formula.
keyPoints: The aim is to determine the formula of hydrated copper sulfate, written CuSO4.xH2O.
Heat gently and stir until the blue salt turns completely white, showing all the water has left.
The water's mass is the hydrated mass minus the anhydrous mass left in the dish.
Divide each mass by its own relative formula mass, then simplify the ratio of water to salt.
Write the answer in the form salt.xH2O, rounding the water count to the nearest whole number.
Avoid overheating: a decomposed salt loses extra mass and corrupts the ratio.

low.restatement: Blue crystals go into the dish, white powder comes out; the missing grams are water. Two divisions by relative formula masses turn salt-mass and water-mass into moles, and the mole ratio writes the formula.
low.analogy: It is like weighing a soggy sponge before and after drying: the difference is the water it held, and weighing the dry sponge separately tells you the sponge's own share.
low.examPointer: Expect an awkward mole ratio: whole numbers are unlikely first time, so round the water figure sensibly at the end.

medium.restatement: Each mass divides by the relative formula mass of what it measures: salt mass by the anhydrous Mr, water mass by eighteen. Simplify the two mole values to a whole-number ratio and stamp it after the salt's formula.
medium.analogy: Two friends split a hotel bill in an odd ratio; divide what each paid by the price of one night and the ratio of nights tells you who stayed how long.
medium.examPointer: State the salt formula with its dot before quoting x: examiners want CuSO4.xH2O-style answers, not a bare number floating alone.

glossary.definition: A salt that carries water within its crystals.
Water locked into a hydrated salt's crystal structure, written into the formula after a dot.
The simplest whole-number ratio of the elements or ions in a compound, deduced here from mole ratios.
The counting unit for amounts of substance; a mass divided by the substance's relative formula mass gives the number of moles.
The difference between the masses recorded before and after heating; in this method it is the water's mass.
Describes the salt left once every trace of its water has been driven off.
The total of the relative atomic masses in a formula; the number masses are divided by to reach moles.

workedExample.prompt: A dish holds 4.88 g of hydrated copper sulfate, CuSO4.xH2O. Gentle heating to constant mass leaves 4.00 g of white anhydrous CuSO4. (Mr: CuSO4 = 159.5, H2O = 18.) a) Calculate the mass of water lost. b) Determine x and write the formula of the hydrated salt.
steps: Ratio of water to salt = 0.049 / 0.025 = 1.96, which rounds to the nearest whole number 2.
The formula of the hydrated salt is CuSO4.2H2O.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) 0.88 g of water. b) x = 2, so the salt is CuSO4.2H2O.
